name: command-base
intent: Encapsulate a request as a self-contained, serializable command object so it can be shipped across a process, queue or network boundary and executed there by an invoker that knows only the command's base contract.
problem: Work must be performed in another process, on another machine, or later - but caller and executor share no call stack: the far side cannot see the caller's types, the two sides are not available at the same time, and the request must survive restarts or a disconnected client. A plain remote call couples both sides to one interface and one moment in time and leaves nothing inspectable when it fails.
context: Applies at a process, machine or trust boundary where requests are queued, scheduled, retried or spread over workers; where producer and consumer can share only a data contract plus one execution entry point; and where the concrete work (render this report, open this valve, rebuild this index) is decided by the sender while the resources to perform it live on the far side.
benefits: The invoker stays generic: it needs one execution entry point and a tag registry, so new work ships as a new command without changing the dispatcher.
The command is a durable value between the two sides - it can be queued, scheduled, prioritised, retried, audited or moved to another worker, none of which a live call frame allows.
Client and worker lifetimes decouple: an offline or restarting client does not lose work, and workers can be added, drained or upgraded while commands wait in the queue.
Behaviour travels with the request's data, so the far side needs no routing table of its own - the tag names the work and the command performs it.
Load smoothing: a burst queues instead of overloading the far side, and the consumption rate is set by the number of workers rather than by the caller.
The boundary becomes testable and auditable: both halves (codec and invoker) can be exercised with recorded envelopes, and the queue itself is the record of what was asked.
tradeoffs: Concrete command classes must exist in compatible versions on both sides: adding a field or renaming a type is a two-sided deployment, and version skew surfaces only at deserialisation time on the far side.

Deserialising a command is executing code: platform serialisers (BinaryFormatter, Java serialization, pickle, Marshal) instantiate classes the payload names, so any unauthorised producer on the queue is a remote-code-execution risk unless codec and tag set are restricted.

Shipping behaviour removes the compiler from the contract: a missing registration, an unknown tag or a stale worker is a runtime failure - often a poison message that retries forever - instead of a build error.
Failures span four layers - codec, queue, dispatcher, receiver - and the sender's stack trace is gone, so diagnosis needs correlation identifiers and structured logging on the far side.

Queue delivery is at-least-once and unordered by default: duplicates, replays and out-of-order commands are normal, so receivers must be idempotent (or de-duplicated) and ordering must be designed per key.

Per-command overhead is real: every request pays serialisation, a queue round trip and deserialisation, which dominates for tiny commands and pushes large payloads out of the message (claim check) rather than into it.
Eventual consistency: the caller cannot observe the result synchronously, and read-model lag (milliseconds to hours) after command execution requires explicit user-experience design.

Schema evolution on a shared wire contract requires forward-compatibility planning: unknown fields must be tolerated, removed fields must not break old senders, and type changes require a migration strategy.

participants.responsibility: Declares the uniform execution entry point and is the serialisation root; carries only the state every command needs.
Binds the parameters of one request to the action the far side performs; data-only and self-contained in the shared wire format.
Constructs the command, fills its state and hands it to the transport; holds no reference to the far side's receiver.
Carries the serialised command durably between the two sides: addressing, store-and-forward, retry and delivery semantics live here.
Reads envelopes, resolves the concrete command from its tag through an allow-list registry, and calls the execution entry point; knows nothing else about the concrete types.
The resource or domain object the command acts on, resolved on the far side from the command's data.

use_cases: Job queues behind web applications: rendering reports or documents, sending notifications, transcoding media - the request is enqueued as a command and executed by worker processes.
Device, shop-floor or plant control: a management station ships commands (open valve, run recipe, move axis) to a controller that executes them locally with its own resources.
Occasionally connected clients (POS, logistics, field inspections): commands queue offline and execute when the link returns.
Server-side batch and administrative work - backups, index rebuilds, cache flushes - triggered from a thin client or a scheduler.
Distributed build or test farms: a coordinator ships unit-of-work commands to agents that own the required toolchain.
Cross-language or cross-team integrations where the command envelope (tag plus payload schema) is the only shared contract.
Approval and audit workflows where each request must exist as an inspectable, replayable record before it executes.
Microservices sagas and long-running business processes: a process manager (saga orchestrator) issues commands to authoritative services, with compensation logic for rollback on failure.
Serverless function orchestration: step functions or workflow engines dispatch typed commands to Lambda/Functions workers that execute them against external resources.
IoT edge command dispatch: a cloud backend sends control commands to edge devices that may be intermittently connected, queued locally and executed when connectivity is available.
Multi-tenant SaaS back-offices: tenant-specific commands are routed to isolated workers, with command-level tenant isolation enforced at the queue and invoker layers.

Ruby/Rails background processing with Sidekiq: the job class name plus JSON arguments are stored as a Redis hash and executed by competing worker processes - the docs therefore mandate simple JSON-safe arguments and re-fetching ActiveRecord records by id inside perform.

Python distributed task queues with Celery: a producer dispatches by task name (app.send_task) so the sender needs no import of the worker's task code; the task-name registry is the tag table and the broker is the transport.

.NET service-bus endpoints with MassTransit: verb-noun command contracts are sent (never published) to a dedicated endpoint and consumed by exactly one consumer per command, with the JSON envelope carrying MessageId, CorrelationId and routing metadata.
avoid_when: The caller needs the result or the exception now: use a request-reply call (Request-Reply over gRPC/HTTP) rather than a fire-and-forget command.
Both sides are the same process and codebase: a plain method call, or the local Command pattern when you need in-process undo or queueing, is simpler than a codec plus a registry.
The receiver already owns the behaviour: if the far side dispatches on message type itself (Command Message, Document Message), send data instead of executable command classes.
Commands would carry secrets or personal data into a durable queue: pass a claim check and let the worker fetch the data under its own authority.
The work is a stream or a large batch where per-command overhead dominates: batch the units or use a data-parallel job or stream processor.
There is exactly one operation and one worker: an endpoint plus a payload type (Gateway or Remote Facade) is less machinery for the same result.

The domain is collaborative and high-contention (multiple users modifying the same aggregate concurrently): CQRS and event sourcing add complexity that only pays off when audit history, temporal queries, and independent read/write scaling are genuine requirements.
The team lacks operational maturity for eventual consistency: schema evolution, projection rebuilds, snapshot strategy, and observable command processing lag require real engineering attention.
anti_patterns: Late-bound or reflective commands that carry an assembly/class/method name plus arguments (the source article labels its own such variant quick and dirty): they turn the queue into an unauthenticated remote-code-execution interface and destroy the type contract.
Platform-native serialisation of arbitrary types (BinaryFormatter, Java serialization, pickle, Marshal) on a queue with more than one producer, so deserialisation instantiates attacker-named classes.
Commands that hold live references - a receiver instance, an open file handle, a database connection - so serialisation drags an object graph (or fails) instead of carrying the receiver's identity.
A god command base: Execute plus Undo, Retry, scheduling, logging and authorisation hooks, forcing every command to implement concerns only one of them has.
Unbounded payloads - whole documents or blobs in the message - instead of a claim check that passes a reference and a checksum.
Non-idempotent commands on an at-least-once queue with no de-duplication, so a retry charges a card twice or re-renders the same file.
Dispatch through a dynamic loader or reflection on the payload's type name, so adding a jar or assembly to the worker silently adds executable commands.

Polymorphic deserialization with enableDefaultTyping or @JsonTypeInfo using class-name resolution on untrusted input: re-introduces the arbitrary class instantiation risk that data-only formats are meant to eliminate.
design_principles: Encapsulation of a request as a first-class object: the request becomes data plus behaviour instead of a stack frame.
Dependency inversion: the invoker depends only on the command contract and a tag registry, never on concrete command types.
Open/closed principle: new work arrives by adding a command and a registry entry on both sides; the invoker stays closed for modification.
Explicit boundary discipline: only serialisable data crosses; live references, handles and object graphs stay behind.
Separation of concerns: the client decides what to do, the queue decides when and where, the invoker decides with which resources.
Uniformity: one execution contract for every request, so queuing, retrying, auditing and monitoring are implemented once for all commands.
Command/Query separation: commands express intent to change state; queries express intent to read state; keeping them in separate models allows independent optimisation of each path.
best_practices: Keep the command base narrow - one execution entry point plus the serialisation contract - and put per-command metadata in the concrete command or the envelope.
Use an explicit, versioned wire contract with stable tags (protobuf/JSON discriminator, @SerialName, serde rename) rather than class names, and let workers tolerate unknown fields.
Treat the queue as untrusted input: authenticate producers, encrypt the channel, allow-list the tag-to-implementation mapping and never deserialise a type the payload names.
Make commands immutable, data-only and self-contained; move large payloads behind a claim check (reference plus checksum).
Design for at-least-once delivery: idempotent receivers or a de-duplication key, a maximum-retry policy and a dead-letter channel for unknown tags and poison messages.
Keep the invoker generic and observable: structured logs with a correlation identifier, per-command metrics, no per-command branching outside the registry.
Test both halves with recorded envelopes (golden codec tests) and a fake transport, so a wire-format change is caught before it reaches a running queue.

Use data-only serialization formats (JSON, Protocol Buffers, MessagePack, CBOR) rather than code-bearing formats (Java Serialization, Python pickle, .NET BinaryFormatter). If native serialization cannot be avoided, enforce an explicit type allow-list at deserialization time.

Distinguish transient from permanent failures in handlers: throw or rethrow transient exceptions (database timeouts, network unavailable) so the transport retries; return normally or use a domain-specific permanent failure type for validation errors so the message is acknowledged and discarded rather than dead-lettered.

Attach correlation identifiers (UUID, trace ID) to every command envelope and propagate them through every log line and downstream call to reconstruct the distributed execution path from the sender's perspective.
Include a TTL or expiration timestamp on time-sensitive commands; handlers should check it and acknowledge without reprocessing if the action is no longer relevant.

Design command handlers to be idempotent using a natural idempotency key (order ID, customer ID) rather than a generated message ID, so that replay and retry produce the same outcome as a single execution.
Monitor dead-letter queue depth as a key operational metric: a rising DLQ indicates a systemic failure (bad deployment, poison message flood, downstream outage) requiring immediate attention.

For long-running workflows spanning multiple services, use a saga or process manager that issues individual commands and coordinates compensation (rollback commands) on failure, rather than embedding the entire workflow in a single god command.

Version the wire contract explicitly: bump a version field or use a schema identifier, and run old and new workers in parallel during rolling deployments so old commands can still be deserialised by new workers and vice versa.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1995) - Command: encapsulate a request as an object, letting you parameterise clients, queue or log requests.

Brad King, "Simplify Distributed System Design Using the Command Pattern, MSMQ, and .NET", MSDN Magazine, September 2004 - a Command base class with one Execute method, queued to an invoker service that deserialises each message and calls Execute.

Martin Fowler, "CQRS", Martin Fowler's Bliki, 2011 - Command Query Responsibility Segregation: using separate models for updating and reading information, fitting naturally with event-based programming models and domain-driven design.

Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Command Message: encapsulating a request as a message so it can be transmitted to a receiver that will execute the requested action.

Amazon Web Services, "Decompose Monoliths into Microservices by Using CQRS and Event Sourcing", AWS Prescriptive Guidance - combining CQRS with event sourcing on AWS using Lambda, DynamoDB, SNS and SQS for independent read/write scaling.

Usama Qamar, "CQRS + Event Sourcing: A Production Architecture Guide", 2026 - practical production architecture combining CQRS and event sourcing: separate read/write models, event-store-as-truth, snapshots, projection rebuilds, and operational trade-offs.

OWASP, "Deserialization Cheat Sheet", OWASP Cheat Sheet Series - prevention and mitigation strategies for deserialization attacks, covering allow-listing, safe serializers, and gadget chain risks across Java, Python, .NET, and PHP.

Microsoft, "Deserialization risks in use of BinaryFormatter and related types", .NET Documentation, 2024 - BinaryFormatter is dangerous and cannot be secured; alternatives include System.Text.Json, XmlSerializer, and DataContractSerializer.

Safeguard.sh, "Insecure Deserialization Explained: Gadget Chains & Fixes" (CVE-502, OWASP A08:2021) - gadget chain exploitation via ysoserial for Java, pickle for Python, BinaryFormatter for .NET; safe alternatives including JSON, Protobuf, MessagePack, and ObjectInputFilter allow-listing.

SecureBlock, "Deserialization of Untrusted Data — Critical Severity (CVSS 9.8)" - language-agnostic deserialization risks in Java (ObjectInputStream), Python (pickle), .NET (BinaryFormatter), PHP (unserialize), Ruby (Marshal); ysoserial and gadget chain mitigation.

Nimbus, "Commands Documentation" - command semantics for queue-based fire-and-forget messaging: one handler per command, imperative naming, idempotent handler design, dead-letter queues, and retry policies.

Axon Framework, "Command Dispatchers Reference" - CommandBus, CommandGateway, and CommandDispatcher interfaces; ProcessingContext propagation for correlation; routing strategies for aggregate-aware command routing in CQRS applications.

NILUS, "Command Routing Strategies in CQRS Microservices" - authoritative bounded-context routing, layered command routing models, Kafka-based asynchronous routing, policy-based routing, anti-corruption layers, and saga orchestration for cross-context commands.

OneUptime, "How to Implement Command Pattern with Dapr" - command pattern with Dapr for microservices: command logging in state stores, idempotent handlers, and correlation ID propagation via Dapr service invocation.

sbooker/command-bus, "Reliable Command Bus for PHP" - persistent, transactional command bus with at-least-once delivery, declarative retry strategies, state tracking (created/pending/success/fail), and foundation for saga/process manager implementations.

FreeSideNomad/jrcmd, "Reliable Command Bus for Spring Boot with PostgreSQL PGMQ" - exactly-once delivery semantics via PGMQ, automatic retry with configurable backoff, troubleshooting queue (TSQ) for operator intervention, batch operations, and process manager for saga orchestration.

iluwatar/java-design-patterns, "Commander Pattern" - retry handling, idempotency checks, queue database, and failover across ShippingService, PaymentService, MessagingService, and EmployeeHandle for distributed transaction resilience.

Vegetam/Saga-pattern-architecture, "Saga Pattern Architecture" - production-grade saga orchestration with Kafka, distributed Redis locks for idempotency, exponential backoff retry, dead letter queues, compensation logic, and observability.

snatalenko/node-cqrs, "CQRS Backbone with Event Sourcing for Node.js" - pluggable RabbitMQ command and event buses, aggregate command handlers, event store with snapshots, distributed sagas with event correlation, and resilient projections with checkpoint and readiness gates.

MediatR library documentation - in-process mediator/dispatcher pattern for .NET: request/handler registration, pipeline behaviours for cross-cutting concerns (logging, validation, retry, audit), and notification-based publish/subscribe.

MassTransit, "Messages" documentation - https://masstransit.io/usage/messages.html - commands as data-only verb-noun contracts sent to one dedicated endpoint with exactly one consumer, versus published past-tense events; the envelope carries MessageId, CorrelationId and routing metadata.

Sidekiq, "Best Practices" wiki - https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/wiki/Best-Practices - pass simple JSON-serialisable arguments (ids, not objects), fetch records inside perform, and design jobs idempotent against retries.

Sidekiq, "Job Format" wiki - https://sidekiq.org/wiki/Job-Format - a queued command on the wire: a Redis hash with class, jid, args and timestamps, executed by worker processes pulling from the queue.

GoatReview, "Don't use MediatR by default on all .NET projects" - https://goatreview.com/dont-use-mediatr-by-default-net-projects/ - criticism of defaulting every use case through a command/mediator bus: chained dispatch from handlers and pervasive indirection as over-engineering.

ddd-cqrs group, "Why lots of developers use one-way command messaging (async handling) when it's not needed?" - https://groups.google.com/g/dddcqrs/c/xhJHVxDx2pM - practitioner critique of asynchronous one-way commands when synchronous handling would return the answer to the caller immediately.
